TK01-q01-3gccg9: 500 gallons is the California flammable-liquid speeding and hours threshold, not the N endorsement tank size.
1,000 gallons or more is the aggregate (total) rule; each individual tank must be more than 119 gallons.
TK01-q02-o3iwvz: The liquid does not have to be HazMat; any liquid or liquid gas, even milk or water, counts.
Flammability is not part of the N endorsement rule; any liquid or liquid gas counts.
TK01-q03-4ff06c: Tires matter on any truck, but on all tank vehicles the most important thing to check for is leaks.
Vapor recovery kits are special equipment to check if equipped, but leaks are the most important item.
TK01-q04-wyukuf: Grounding and bonding cables are on the tanker special purpose list, so they must be checked if equipped.
Emergency shutoff systems are on the tanker special purpose list, so they must be checked if equipped.
TK01-q05-r46y4m: Backwards: tankers have a high center of gravity, which makes them top-heavy and easy to roll over.
Some tanks do lack baffles, but rollover risk comes from weight riding high off the road.
TK01-q06-ai30az: Tests show tankers can roll over even at the posted curve speed, not only when speeding.
Rollovers are tied to the high center of gravity and curve speed; tests show rollovers at the posted curve speed.
TK01-q07-5mpq36: Expansion as liquid warms is why you leave outage; surge is liquid moving in a partly filled tank.
Surge has nothing to do with vents; it is liquid moving back and forth in a partly filled tank.
TK01-q08-6y5wf8: The wave pushes the truck in the direction the wave moves, and can shove it into the intersection.
Surge still acts on a stopped truck; on ice the wave can shove it into an intersection.
TK01-q09-da2nod: That describes bulkheads; baffles are bulkheads with holes that let liquid flow through.
Food tankers usually have no baffles at all, because sanitation rules forbid them.
TK01-q10-hta901: Baffles do not stop all surge; side-to-side surge can still happen and cause a rollover.
Surge comes from a partly filled tank; in a baffled tank the surge still possible is side-to-side.
TK01-q11-fkzl1t: With bulkheads the rule is to watch weight distribution; never load a cargo tank totally full.
Bulkheads are solid walls with no holes; there are no baffles to open, so watch weight distribution.
TK01-q12-b62b5o: Taste is not the reason; baffles make the tank hard to clean, so sanitation rules forbid them.
Milk surges like any liquid; smooth bore tanks actually have the strongest forward-and-back surge.
TK01-q13-6tycyn: Steady freeway driving is not the main danger; strong forward-and-back surge hits when starting and stopping.
Surge comes from a partly filled tank; smooth bore tanks are most dangerous when starting and stopping.
TK01-q14-kiseit: The reason is expansion: liquids expand as they warm, so you must leave outage.
Vents are not the reason; liquids expand as they warm, so the tank needs room (outage).
TK01-q15-6hni5w: Surge is liquid moving in a partly filled tank, not the space left for expansion.
Aggregate is the total capacity of all tanks, not the space left for expansion.
TK01-q16-ffmogc: Legal weight limits are one of the things that decide how much liquid to load.
The weight of the liquid is one of the things that decide how much to load.
TK01-q17-5tc2hg: Length and dead axles are not the tanker reasons; they are the high center of gravity and liquid surge.
Air brakes and converter dollies belong to other sections; tankers need care for high center of gravity and surge.
TK01-q18-y69hwg: Releasing the brakes too soon lets the surge wave push the truck forward; keep steady pressure.
Pumping hard is not the rule; keep steady pressure and brake far ahead of the stop.
TK01-q19-a22d9e: Steering quickly while braking can roll the tanker over; use controlled or stab braking.
Steering while braking can roll a tanker; use controlled or stab braking without quick steering.
TK01-q20-jg7asn: The posted curve speed may be too fast for a tanker; slow down before the curve, not in it.
Slow down before the curve, then accelerate slightly through it; coasting is not the handbook method.
TK01-q21-d3xqyb: The handbook says the opposite: an empty tanker may take longer to stop than a full one.
Wet roads double the normal stopping distance.
TK01-q22-80f394: Wet roads change stopping distance a lot: they double it.
Wet roads make stopping distance longer, not shorter: they double it.
TK01-q23-liinnx: 1,000 gallons is the aggregate N endorsement number; a CLP holder may drive only an empty tank.
Any load counts; a CLP holder may drive a tank vehicle only if it is empty (purged if it held HazMat).
TK01-q24-lwi8qp: More than 119 gallons is the individual-tank N endorsement rule, not the 10-hour limit threshold.
1,000 gallons or more is the aggregate N endorsement rule, not the 10-hour limit threshold.
TK01-q25-b8g36a: Adding N to an existing Class C needs the applicable knowledge tests only, not a skills test.
Only a new Class C applicant with N alone needs a skills test; adding N to a Class C needs knowledge tests only.
TK01-q26-o6y1ug: A skid does not cause a leak; on tank trailers, a drive or trailer wheel skid can cause a jackknife.
Baffles only slow surge; they cannot stop a skid, and a skidding tank trailer may jackknife.
